q: What equipment and teaware is essential for brewing tea?
What is the difference between a teapot and a tea kettle?
What types of teapots are used for different teas?
What is a gaiwan and how is it used for brewing tea?
What is a Yixing clay teapot and why is it special?
What is a kyusu teapot and what teas is it used for?
What materials are teapots made from and how do they affect flavor?
What is a tetsubin (iron kettle) and how is it used?
a: Tea brewing equipment ranges from simple single-steep vessels to elaborate multi-piece gongfu sets. A gaiwan (lidded bowl) is the most versatile tea brewing vessel—consisting of a bowl, lid, and saucer—used for brewing any type of tea with easy leaf viewing, aroma appreciation, and precise control over steeping time. Yixing clay teapots (from Yixing, China) are unglazed, porous, purple-sand (zisha) vessels that absorb tea oils over years of use, slowly seasoning to enhance the flavor of a specific tea type—serious collectors maintain separate pots for different tea categories (one for sheng pu-erh, one for shou pu-erh, one for oolong, one for red tea) because the seasoned pot would interfere with other tea flavors. A kyusu is a traditional Japanese side-handled teapot, typically made of glazed or unglazed Tokoname clay, with a built-in ceramic mesh strainer, designed primarily for Japanese green teas like sencha and gyokuro. A tetsubin (cast-iron kettle) is used for heating water (not for brewing tea directly) and can add trace minerals to the water that soften it and enhance tea flavor—authentic tetsubin are lined with enamel to prevent rust, while decorative cast-iron teapots (often sold as tetsubin) should not be confused with true water-heating kettles. The choice of teaware material—porcelain (neutral, ideal for delicate teas), stoneware (good heat retention, versatile), glass (visually beautiful but loses heat quickly, ideal for blooming teas), clay (flavor-enhancing with seasoning), and silver (excellent heat conduction and purity)—affects brewing temperature, heat retention, and the flavor profile of the brewed tea.

q: What are tea cups and how are they selected for different teas?
What is the difference between a cha hai (fairness pitcher) and a gong dao bei?
What is a tea boat and why is it used?
What is a tea strainer and when is it needed?
What are tea pets in Chinese tea culture?
What is a tea tray and how is it used in gongfu cha?
What are tea utensils and tools (cha ju) for gongfu brewing?
What is a tea scoop or cha ze for measuring tea?
a: Tea cups in traditional Chinese and Japanese tea culture are small, typically holding only 30-90 ml (1-3 ounces) to allow frequent re-steeping and appreciation of both aroma and flavor evolution across multiple infusions. A cha hai (tea sea), also called gong dao bei (fairness pitcher), is a small glass or ceramic pitcher that receives the decanted tea from the teapot or gaiwan, ensuring uniform strength among all cups before pouring—this is essential in gongfu tea service where multiple guests receive tea from shared subsequent infusions. A tea boat (cha chuan) is a shallow ceramic or stoneware vessel that holds the teapot and cups, often with a perforated surface that allows wastewater and rinsing water to drain into the lower compartment—it keeps the tea table dry and organized during multi-steep sessions. Tea pets (cha chong) are small unglazed clay figurines placed on the tea tray that absorb tea poured over them as a ritual offering, developing a rich patina over years of use—popular shapes include frogs (prosperity), dragons (power), and lucky cats. The full set of gongfu tea tools (cha ju) includes the cha ze (tea scoop for measuring leaves), cha bi (tea brush for cleaning the tray), cha xian (tea needle for clearing the teapot spout), cha jia (tea tongs for handling cups), cha lou (tea funnel for guiding leaves into narrow-mouthed pots), and cha chi (tea spoon for removing used leaves)—these tools are often displayed in a wooden tool holder (cha tong) that keeps them organized and accessible during the ceremony.

q: What is a tea infuser and what types are available?
What is the best tea infuser for loose leaf tea?
What is a tea ball vs a basket infuser?
What is a tea filter or tea bag?
What is a French press for tea?
What are disposable tea filters and how are they used?
What is an infuser mug or travel tea mug?
What is a tea sock or tea syrup maker?
a: Tea infusers come in many forms, and the best choice depends on the tea type and brewing vessel. Basket infusers (perforated stainless steel or silicone mesh baskets that sit inside a teapot or mug) are generally preferred for whole-leaf teas because they allow ample room for the leaves to expand and fully unfurl—critical for high-quality teas where flavor extraction depends on water circulation around the leaves. Tea balls (perforated metal spheres on a chain) are compact and portable but cramped, making them suitable only for broken-leaf teas and herbal blends—full-leaf teas cannot expand properly in a cramped ball, resulting in weaker flavor. Silicone infusers (often novelty-shaped like animals or geometric forms) offer creative presentation but have fewer and larger holes that can let fine tea particles through. Disposable paper tea filters (empty filter bags you fill and seal) are convenient for single servings and easy cleanup but create waste. An infuser mug—a mug with an integrated basket infuser and lid—is ideal for office or travel brewing where a full teapot is impractical. French press teapots, while designed for coffee, make excellent brewers for large-leaf teas and herbals because the plunger filter keeps leaves contained while allowing full water contact and easy separation. For best results with any infuser, use water at the appropriate temperature for the tea type, leave enough headroom for the leaves to expand (at least 2-3 times the dry leaf volume), and remove the infuser after the recommended steeping time to prevent over-extraction and bitterness.

q: What is the gongfu tea ceremony and how is it performed?
What equipment is needed for gongfu cha?
What is the correct tea-to-water ratio for gongfu brewing?
What are the steps of the gongfu tea ceremony?
How many infusions can you get from gongfu brewing?
What teas are best suited for gongfu cha?
What is the rinse (first steep) in gongfu cha?
How does gongfu brewing differ from western-style brewing?
a: Gongfu cha (Kung Fu tea) is a traditional Chaozhou/Chaoshan-style Chinese tea preparation that emphasizes multiple short, concentrated infusions using a high leaf-to-water ratio to extract the full flavor evolution of the tea across many steeps—typically 8-15 infusions for high-quality oolong, pu-erh, or aged white teas. The setup includes a gaiwan or small Yixing pot (typically 100-150 ml), a cha hai/gong dao bei (fairness pitcher), small tasting cups (pin ming bei) and aromatic cups (wen xiang bei—tall cups used with Tefu/Gaoshan oolongs), a tea tray, and a kettle with temperature-controlled water. The standard gongfu process: (1) warm the teaware with hot water, (2) add tea leaves (approximately 5-8 grams per 100 ml of water—a very high ratio compared to western-style 1-2 grams per 250 ml), (3) rinse the leaves with a quick pour and immediate discard (to 'awaken' the leaves and remove dust), (4) steep for the first infusion (10-25 seconds for high-mountain oolongs, increasing by 5-10 seconds per subsequent steep), (5) decant into the fairness pitcher, (6) pour into tasting cups, and (7) enjoy, appreciating the aroma, flavor, mouthfeel, and aftertaste of each evolving infusion. The key difference from western-style brewing (a longer single steep with fewer leaves) is that gongfu reveals the tea's character progressively—the first few infusions are light and floral, middle infusions reach full body and complexity, and later infusions reveal subtle sweetness and lingering finish that would be lost in a single long steep.

q: What tea storage equipment is essential for keeping tea fresh?
What is a tea caddy and what types exist?
What are the best containers for storing different teas?
What is a pu-erh tea storage container or storage box?
How should I store matcha powder?
What is a tea canister for daily use?
How do I store tea for long-term aging?
What are Mylar bags and oxygen absorbers for tea storage?
a: Proper tea storage equipment protects tea from the four enemies: light, heat, air (oxygen), and moisture (humidity). The ideal storage container is airtight, opaque, and made of food-grade, non-reactive material—popular options include double-sealed ceramic tea caddies (Japanese natsume for matcha or Chinese tea canisters with airtight silicone seals), light-proof tin or aluminum tins, and UV-protective glass jars (for display, though these should be kept in a dark cabinet). Matcha requires special storage in a cool, dark place (preferably refrigerated in an airtight container) after opening because its finely ground surface area makes it extremely susceptible to oxidation—ceramic natsume caddies are the traditional matcha container, but modern storage often uses vacuum-sealed bags or resealable Mylar pouches. Pu-erh tea differs from other teas in requiring active, breathable storage (not airtight) to facilitate microbial aging—traditional pu-erh storage uses unglazed clay jars or bamboo baskets in humidity-controlled environments (60-70% relative humidity for tropical-style aging in China and Southeast Asia), with the tea separated by type (sheng vs shou) to prevent flavor cross-contamination. For long-term aging of any tea, Mylar bags with zip closures (with most air pressed out) inside food-grade buckets or tins, stored in a cool (below 70°F/21°C), dark place with stable humidity (50-60% RH), can preserve freshness for years—adding oxygen absorbers is recommended only for fully dried teas (not for pu-erh or partially oxidized teas) since complete oxygen removal can suppress the beneficial aging reactions. The golden rule is that tea is hygroscopic (absorbs moisture and odors from the environment), so never store tea in the refrigerator or freezer alongside strongly aromatic foods unless it is in a completely sealed, impermeable container.
